analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue police for misconduct, restricts chokeholds and no-knock warrants, and creates a national misconduct registry.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 136 Democratic cosponsors after its September 2025 introduction but has seen no committee action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it easier to hold police officers accountable in court, ban or restrict certain policing tactics like chokeholds and no-knock drug warrants, and create a public national registry of police misconduct records. It would also require federal, state, and local agencies to collect and publish data on stops, searches, and use of force, with federal grant money cut off for agencies that do not comply. It was introduced in September 2025 and referred to three House committees, where no action has been taken.
analysis.who_benefits: People who say they were harmed by police misconduct would find it easier to sue officers and recover damages, since the bill narrows the qualified immunity defense [S2]. Communities that experience racial profiling would gain a private right to sue over it, and the public would gain access to a searchable national database of police misconduct records, plus uniform federal reporting on use of force, stops, and searches [S2]. States and tribes that adopt independent investigation procedures would receive federal grant money [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would let victims of police misconduct sue more easily by limiting the qualified immunity defense that often ends civil cases before trial, and lower the criminal intent standard for convicting officers in federal prosecutions from 'willful' to 'knowing or reckless'.

It would create a public, searchable National Police Misconduct Registry of complaints, discipline records, and lawsuit settlements, so that officers fired for misconduct in one department could not quietly be hired by another.

It would ban no-knock warrants in drug cases, restrict chokeholds and carotid holds, and set a national standard limiting use of force to circumstances where it is necessary, backed by training requirements on de-escalation and the duty of officers to intervene against excessive force.

It would create a private right of action against racial profiling with disparate-impact proof, and require all law enforcement agencies to report stops, searches, and use of force broken down by race, ethnicity, and gender, with federal grants cut off from states that fail to report.

It would give the Justice Department subpoena power in pattern-or-practice investigations and let state attorneys general bring those suits too, plus fund independent investigations of police killings at the state level.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the grant programs (over $900 million authorized across fiscal years 2026-2028 in the bill text). Law enforcement agencies and their insurers would bear higher legal liability costs as qualified immunity is limited, and state and local departments would take on new data-collection and accreditation duties, with federal grant money withheld if they do not comply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; police departments and unions

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes more than $900 million in new grant spending over fiscal years 2026-2028 (for example, $750 million for independent investigations and $100 million a year for state pattern-or-practice investigations), an ongoing federal cost.

Critics of qualified immunity reform argue that removing the good-faith defense could expose individual officers and their municipalities to costly lawsuits for split-second decisions, which supporters of the defense say could discourage people from policing or make departments harder to insure; the bill does not address how those costs would be absorbed.

The bill leans heavily on conditioning federal Byrne and COPS grant money on compliance — a funding penalty that falls partly on state and local budgets, and that could leave residents of noncomplying states with both the misconduct problem and less grant money.
A public, searchable registry of officer misconduct records raises employment-privacy concerns for officers, which the bill only partially addresses through Privacy Act protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — making officers answerable in court and giving the public hard data on policing practices — addresses an accountability gap that ordinary legal remedies currently fail to close, since qualified immunity frequently blocks lawsuits regardless of the merits. The costs are real but mostly fiscal (roughly $900 million in authorized grants) or borne by departments through compliance work, and the liability concerns, while serious for officers and municipal budgets, are the intended mechanism of deterrence rather than a side effect. The design is more carrot-and-stick than mandate, which keeps it constitutionally straightforward but also means its force depends entirely on grant conditions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2025 and sent to three House committees, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, nothing scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Ivey introduced the bill on September 15, 2025, with 136 House Democrats as original cosponsors and no Republicans.
The Speaker referred it to three committees at once — Judiciary, Armed Services, and Energy and Commerce — which means any one of them can hold it without a deadline.
No hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled or recorded in any of the three committees since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position: law enforcement agencies and unions continue to operate under existing rules, and the people the bill aims to protect have gained nothing. The status quo persists because the bill has not moved in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current policing rules remain unchanged

for.name: Rep. Glenn Ivey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the cosponsors

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican member signed on as a cosponsor, and the three committees the bill was referred to are chaired by the majority party, which controls whether it ever gets a hearing or a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 136 cosponsors are House Democrats and no Republican has signed on, leaving the bill a one-party effort in a Congress where Republicans control both chambers.

industries.industry: Law enforcement unions and officer professional interests (e.g., Fraternal Order of Police)
industries.note: The bill lowers the criminal intent standard for federal prosecutions, limits qualified immunity, and creates a public registry of officer misconduct records — directly raising the legal and career costs of misconduct for officers and the unions that bargain for them.

Departments would face new reporting, accreditation, and certification duties, with Byrne and COPS grant money withheld for noncompliance, and higher liability exposure from limited qualified immunity.

The bill pushes agencies toward accreditation and requires 5 percent of certain federal grant awards to be spent on gaining or maintaining it, creating a steady funding stream for accreditation bodies.

industries.industry: Body camera and in-car video manufacturers
industries.note: The bill requires body cameras for federal officers and cameras in patrol vehicles, creating a new guaranteed government market.
The Stop Militarizing Law Enforcement Act provisions would restrict transfers of military equipment to local police, shrinking that market.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action more than two months after referral, the bill is likely to sit in committee for the rest of this Congress unless its provisions are attached to a larger, must-pass bill. A standalone version has not reached a floor vote in any Congress since 2020.
